title: Trump Said “I Understand Money Better Than Anybody” During a 2016 Campaign Interview
description_short: Trump said “I understand money better than anybody” during a 2016 campaign interview
description_medium: During a June 21, 2016 interview about campaign fundraising and self-funding, Donald Trump said, “I understand money better than anybody.” The reviewed reporting supports that wording and context, not the original phrase “anyone that’s ever lived” or unrelated claims about business losses, taxes, or policy arguments.
description_long: Donald Trump made the “I understand money better than anybody” remark during a June 21, 2016 interview about how he would finance his general-election campaign. A contemporaneous TODAY report and broadcast transcript place the line in a discussion of fundraising, not a detailed economic-policy proposal. Trump said he had spent $55 million of his own money to win the primaries, said he might do the same in the general election, and complained that Republican officials had been slow to support him. He also said he could win without the party’s help but would welcome it. Read in the original exchange, the boast served as part of his argument about his financial independence and campaign resources. The interview documents what he claimed about his spending and fundraising; it does not independently verify the $55 million figure or establish the accuracy of his wider economic claims.

title: Reuters Reports USAID Staffing Plan to Retain 294 and Rubio’s Claim That Over 80% of Programs Were Canceled
description_short: Reuters reported a plan to retain 294 of over 10,000 USAID staff; Rubio said more than 80% of programs were canceled
description_medium: Reuters reported in February 2025 that the administration planned to retain 294 of USAID’s more than 10,000 worldwide staff. On March 10, Secretary of State Marco Rubio said over 80% of agency programs had been canceled and remaining programs would move to State. These were a reported staffing plan and Rubio’s attributed program figure, not an audited count of 10,000 completed firings or the end of all U.S. foreign aid.
description_long: Reuters reported on February 6, 2025 that the administration planned to retain 294 of USAID’s more than 10,000 staff worldwide. The report described a planned workforce and related leave or contractor actions; it did not establish that every other employee had already been fired. On March 10, Secretary of State Marco Rubio said that more than 80% of USAID programs had been canceled and that roughly 1,000 remaining programs would be administered by the State Department. The staffing number was a reported plan, while the cancellation percentage was Rubio’s attributed statement, not an independently audited total in these reports. The figures document a major planned contraction and program review, but do not show that all U.S. foreign assistance ended. The administration said some programs would continue under State. This entry distinguishes staffing from programs, plans from completed separations, and a public official’s account from an independently verified count.

preserved_fields.title: Trump Administration Moves to Dismantle USAID Workforce and Cancels Most Agency Programs
preserved_fields.description_short: Trump Administration Moves to Dismantle USAID Workforce and Cancels Most Agency Programs
preserved_fields.description_medium: The Trump administration sharply reduced USAID's workforce and foreign-assistance portfolio in early 2025. In February, officials planned to retain only a few hundred of more than 10,000 USAID staff, while many employees were placed on leave and some positions were eliminated. On March 10, Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the administration had cancelled about 83% of USAID programs, leaving roughly 1,000 to continue under State Department oversight. The stored claim that DOGE fired approximately 10,000 workers and ended all U.S. foreign aid is inaccurate.

title: Trump FY2018 Budget Proposes $610 Billion in Medicaid Savings
description_short: Trump’s FY2018 budget proposed $610 billion in Medicaid savings over ten years
description_medium: The Trump administration’s May 2017 FY2018 budget request proposed about $610 billion in Medicaid savings over ten years through Medicaid reforms. Separately, CBO estimated that the House-passed American Health Care Act would reduce Medicaid outlays by about $834 billion over ten years. These are estimates for different proposals, not enacted cuts or one combined figure.
description_long: The Trump administration’s May 2017 FY2018 budget request proposed about $610 billion in Medicaid savings over ten years through reforms that would give states per-capita-cap or block-grant options. The House-passed American Health Care Act was separate legislation; CBO estimated that it would reduce Medicaid outlays by about $834 billion over ten years. The amounts should not be collapsed into a single $800 billion administration-budget figure or described as realized savings. A presidential budget request outlines proposals and does not itself change Medicaid funding; congressional action would have been required. The sources support the proposal amounts and their distinct origins, but do not establish later actual spending reductions or the effects on particular beneficiaries. This entry records the administration’s budget proposal and identifies the separate congressional estimate so readers can distinguish the two baselines and legislative vehicles. These figures are estimates, not observed reductions in Medicaid enrollment or services.
notes: Correction applied: distinguishes the budget’s roughly $610 billion in additional savings from the House bill’s separate roughly $839 billion estimate.

proposed_claim: Trump FY2018 Budget Proposes $610 Billion in Medicaid Savings

unsupported_original_claims: The May 23, 2017 administration budget itself proposed more than $800 billion in Medicaid cuts.

title: ICE Arrests Columbia Protest Organizer Mahmoud Khalil; Deportation Temporarily Blocked
description_short: ICE Arrests Columbia Protest Organizer Mahmoud Khalil for Deportation Proceedings
description_medium: Reuters reported that DHS agents arrested Columbia graduate student and protest organizer Mahmoud Khalil on March 8, 2025, and that his union said he held a green card. A judge temporarily blocked his deportation the next day while proceedings continued. The reports do not establish that officials admitted a speech-only motive or that the case had a final legal outcome.
description_long: Reuters reported that Department of Homeland Security agents arrested Mahmoud Khalil at his Columbia University residence on March 8, 2025. The report described him as a prominent pro-Palestinian protest organizer and said his union reported that he held U.S. permanent-resident status. A second Reuters report said a federal judge temporarily blocked his deportation while the proceedings continued and that he was moved to Louisiana. These reports document an arrest, reported status, and temporary court order; they do not establish the original entry’s claim that officials admitted the arrest was based entirely on political speech or that Khalil had committed no crime. Characterizations by Khalil’s lawyers or advocacy groups should be attributed to them rather than presented as government admissions or judicial findings. The cited coverage does not establish the final outcome of the immigration case. The event is therefore limited to the arrest and temporary judicial intervention, with motive and ultimate legality left open.

preserved_fields.title: ICE Arrests Columbia Protest Organizer Mahmoud Khalil for Deportation Proceedings
preserved_fields.description_short: ICE Arrests Columbia Protest Organizer Mahmoud Khalil for Deportation Proceedings

The administration sought his removal under a provision allowing the secretary of state to determine that a noncitizen's presence could adversely affect U.S. foreign policy. Khalil and his lawyers argued that the action punished protected political speech. Those competing positions should be attributed rather than collapsed into a government admission.

title: Trump FY2026 Budget Proposes Eliminating the Legal Services Corporation
description_short: Trump’s FY2026 budget sought to eliminate LSC and included $21 million for close-out costs
description_medium: The White House’s May 30, 2025 FY2026 budget proposal sought to eliminate the Legal Services Corporation and requested $21 million for close-out costs; LSC received $560 million in FY2025. Congress later enacted $540 million for FY2026 in Public Law 119-74. The February 2025 claim of completed defunding is inaccurate.
description_long: The Legal Services Corporation received a $560 million congressional appropriation for fiscal year 2025. In its May 30, 2025 FY2026 budget request, the Trump administration proposed eliminating LSC and requested $21 million for close-out costs. That request was a proposal, not a February 2025 cancellation of existing funding. Congress later enacted $540 million for LSC for FY2026 in Public Law 119-74, which specifies the amount and its program allocations. The enacted appropriation means the administration’s proposal did not become complete defunding. The supplied sources do not quantify any service reductions caused by the proposal or show that legal-aid offices immediately lost all federal support. This entry records the budget request, existing FY2025 appropriation, and later enacted FY2026 amount as distinct actions, without inferring that the proposal itself changed grants or ended services. The statute does not prove that no offices experienced disruption.
notes: Missing descriptions composed from supplied event facts, correction constraints and supported procedural distinctions; existing populated descriptions retained exactly.

proposed_claim: Trump FY2026 Budget Proposes Eliminating the Legal Services Corporation

supported_facts: LSC had $560 million in FY2025 congressional funding.
The Trump administration proposed eliminating LSC in its May 30, 2025 FY2026 budget request, with $21 million for close-out costs if approved.
Congress later provided $540 million for LSC in FY2026; therefore the administration proposal did not become a complete defunding.

A presidential budget proposal is not itself an enacted rescission or cancellation of existing grants.
The sources do not establish that legal-aid organizations had already lost all federal support or immediately ceased services.

title: Treasury Announces June 2025 Counterterrorism Designations, Including Addameer
description_short: Treasury designated specific organizations on June 10, 2025, citing alleged militant links
description_medium: On June 10, 2025, Treasury added specific individuals and organizations, including Addameer, to OFAC’s sanctions list. OFAC’s notice links Addameer to the Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine; Reuters described the action as sanctions against named charities over alleged Hamas and PFLP support. The sources do not establish a blanket designation of pro-Palestinian advocacy groups or prosecutions for protected speech.
description_long: On June 10, 2025, the Treasury Department’s Office of Foreign Assets Control announced counterterrorism designations and added named individuals and organizations to the Specially Designated Nationals list. The official notice lists Addameer Prisoner Support and Human Rights Association and identifies a link to the Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine; other named entities are listed with links to Hamas or associated individuals. Reuters reported the action as sanctions against specific charities over alleged support for Hamas and the PFLP. The notice records the government’s designation and stated links; it is not an independent adjudication that every allegation is true. The supplied sources do not support the original broad claim that pro-Palestinian advocacy organizations generally were designated as terrorist-adjacent, nor do they establish tax-status threats or prosecutions of members solely for protected speech. The corrected entry confines itself to the dated sanctions action and named entities, attributing the alleged militant connections to Treasury.
